lesson.title: Two Receptors Are Better Than One: Dimerization and the RTK Signaling Switch
lesson.summary: Receptor tyrosine kinases are single-pass membrane receptors that switch on their own enzymatic activity when ligand binding brings two receptor molecules together, triggering autophosphorylation and launching cascades such as the RAS-MAPK pathway.
lesson.body:
Receptor tyrosine kinases, abbreviated RTKs, are a second major family of enzyme linked cell surface receptors, structurally very different from G protein-coupled receptors. Each RTK molecule is a single polypeptide with just one membrane spanning segment, an extracellular domain that binds a specific ligand, such as a growth factor or insulin, and an intracellular tail that carries tyrosine kinase enzyme activity, meaning it can transfer a phosphate group from ATP onto tyrosine residues of a protein. Unlike GPCRs, a single RTK molecule sitting alone in the membrane is essentially inactive on its own.

The defining event in RTK activation is dimerization. When a ligand binds the extracellular domain of one RTK molecule, it typically causes that receptor to pair up with a second, identical or closely related RTK molecule that has also bound ligand, forming a dimer. Bringing the two cytoplasmic tails into close proximity allows each receptor's kinase domain to phosphorylate tyrosine residues on its partner, a process called autophosphorylation because the receptor pair is essentially phosphorylating itself rather than a separate substrate. This is a direct extension of the ligand-receptor binding principle that binding drives a conformational change, except here the relevant change is bringing two whole receptor molecules together rather than reshaping just one.

The phosphorylated tyrosines on the activated RTK dimer do not do the signaling work themselves; instead they act as docking sites. A range of relay proteins recognize and bind these specific phosphotyrosine sites, and one particularly well studied outcome is activation of the small G protein RAS. Once RAS is switched into its active, GTP bound state, it triggers a cascade of protein kinases, often called the RAS-MAPK pathway, in which each activated kinase phosphorylates and activates the next kinase in line, eventually reaching the nucleus and altering gene expression to drive processes like cell growth and division. This chain of one enzyme activating the next is the same phosphorylation cascade logic examined in more detail later in this chapter.

Insulin signaling illustrates why this mechanism matters physiologically: insulin is a peptide hormone that binds the insulin receptor, itself an RTK that is already a dimer even before ligand binds, and ligand binding reorients the two subunits to trigger autophosphorylation and downstream signaling that promotes glucose uptake into cells. Because RTK pathways so directly control cell growth and division, mutations that cause RTKs to dimerize and signal even without ligand present are a well documented mechanism behind several cancers, underscoring how tightly the normal dimerization requirement must be controlled in healthy cells.

Comparing RTKs to GPCRs highlights two different engineering solutions to the same underlying problem posed by cell surface receptors generally, detecting a signal that cannot cross the membrane and converting it into an intracellular change. GPCRs rely on a separate G protein switch and typically generate diffusible second messengers, while RTKs build the enzymatic switch directly into the receptor itself and generate a signal through direct protein-protein docking and a kinase cascade. Both strategies are reversible, both are specific to their ligand because of the same structural principles covered under ligand-receptor binding, and both ultimately depend on the phosphorylation chemistry that recurs throughout intracellular signaling.
